summary: This is an MDN Web Docs reference page for the JavaScript Array.prototype.sort() method, which sorts array elements in place and returns the same array reference. It covers the default string-based sort order, the compareFn parameter and its required properties, sparse arrays and array-like objects, and stability guaranteed since ECMAScript 2019. Examples include numeric sorting, sorting objects, localeCompare for non-ASCII strings, the map-based sorting pattern, and inconsistent results from malformed comparators across engines. Website navigation and boilerplate are ignored.
one_line: MDN reference for JavaScript's Array.prototype.sort() method, covering default string ordering, comparator functions, stability, and examples.
key_facts: Array.prototype.sort() sorts the elements of an array in place and returns the reference to the same array, now sorted.
The default sort order is ascending, built upon converting the elements into strings, then comparing their sequences of UTF-16 code units values.
The page states that Array.prototype.sort() has been Baseline Widely available since July 2015.
A compareFn returning a negative value indicates that a should come before b; a positive value indicates that a should come after b.
The expression (a, b) => a - b sorts numbers in ascending order.
In a default sort, "80" comes before "9" because numbers are converted to strings and compared in Unicode order.
All undefined elements are sorted to the end of the array, and sort() preserves empty slots by moving them to the end.
To sort without mutating the original array, the note recommends using toSorted(), or a shallow copy such as [...numbers].sort().
Since version 10 (ECMAScript 2019), the specification dictates that Array.prototype.sort is stable.
V8 and JavaScriptCore would not sort the array [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9] with the comparator (a, b) => (a > b ? 1 : 0), while SpiderMonkey returns [1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9].
For strings with non-ASCII characters such as accented letters, the page recommends String.prototype.localeCompare().
The page notes that the compareFn can be invoked multiple times per element, and that the map-based approach can be more efficient; an open source library called mapsort applies this approach.
The page states that the sort() method reads the length property of this and writes back sorted integer-keyed properties, deleting trailing properties when positions are missing.
